analysis.one_liner: Bans new offshore oil and gas leasing off Southern California's coast.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: after its sponsor introduced it in May 1991, it sat in committee and a subcommittee until Congress adjourned in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred the Interior Department from issuing any new offshore oil and gas leases on tracts in the Santa Maria Basin and the Santa Barbara Channel off California's coast [S3]. It would have permanently protected the tracts around the Channel Islands National Marine Sanctuary and blocked leasing on 87 other tracts until 2001 [S2][S3]. The Interior Department had listed those tracts for possible leasing in its draft 1992-1997 offshore drilling program [S3]. The bill was referred to a House committee and then a subcommittee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 102nd Congress ended [S5][S1].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, fishing businesses, and tourism in the Santa Barbara and Channel Islands region would gain protection from the risk of new offshore drilling, spills, and platform construction along their coastline [S2][S3]. Beachgoers and residents of the California coast would benefit from the land being kept off the leasing market [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill permanently prohibited the Secretary of the Interior from issuing any new oil and gas lease on specified tracts off California, including submerged lands within 3 to 6 miles of the Channel Islands National Marine Sanctuary [S3].

It imposed a temporary ban, until January 1, 2001, on new leases for the 87 tracts in the Santa Maria Basin and Santa Barbara Channel that the Interior Department had listed for consideration in its draft 1992-1997 offshore leasing program [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that could have bid on the listed offshore tracts would lose access, and the federal government would forgo potential lease revenue and royalties from new drilling in the Santa Maria Basin and Santa Barbara Channel [S2][S3]. Consumers would bear a negligible share through any effect on domestic oil supply [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies seeking new leases

drawbacks.text: Blocking the 87 tracts would forgo domestic oil and gas production and the federal lease bonuses and royalties that leasing in the Santa Maria Basin and Santa Barbara Channel could have generated [S2][S3].
The permanent prohibition in section 2 would remove those tracts from leasing with no mechanism for revisiting the decision, even if energy or fiscal conditions changed substantially [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people along the California coast, the protection of the Channel Islands sanctuary area and the Santa Barbara Channel from new drilling outweighed the modest national cost of forgone production, since the region had experienced the 1969 Santa Barbara oil spill and drilling there carries concentrated local risk. The cost, in forgone royalties and a small amount of domestic supply, is real but diffuse. The permanent ban on the sanctuary tracts is the strongest part of the bill; the 2001 sunset on the other tracts was a reasonable compromise.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Interior and Insular Affairs Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, but the subcommittee and full committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Lagomarsino of California introduced the bill on May 9, 1991, joined by Rep. Elton Gallegly of California, and it was referred to the House Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs [S1][S5].
On May 21, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water, Power and Offshore Energy Resources, where no further action was recorded [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, without the bill ever being reported out of committee or brought to a vote in the House [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies retained the possibility of leasing in the Santa Maria Basin and Santa Barbara Channel tracts that the Interior Department had listed in its draft 1992-1997 program, and the federal treasury did not lose potential lease revenue. Coastal communities did not get the statutory protection the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies and coastal-lease interests

for.name: Rep. Robert J. Lagomarsino
for.role: U.S. Representative, California's 19th District; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban new offshore oil and gas leasing in the Santa Maria Basin, the Santa Barbara Channel, and the Channel Islands sanctuary area off California.

against.name: House Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. George Miller (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Water, Power and Offshore Energy Resources on May 21, 1991, and never reported it to the House floor.

against.name: Department of the Interior
against.role: Federal agency that manages Outer Continental Shelf leasing under the George H.W. Bush administration
against.what_they_did: Its draft 1992-1997 offshore leasing program identified the 87 Santa Maria Basin and Santa Barbara Channel tracts for oil and gas leasing consideration, which the bill sought to block.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. The only members on record were two California Republicans, the sponsor and the cosponsor, so the partisan shape of support and opposition cannot be measured from the record.

industries.industry: Offshore oil and gas drilling companies
industries.note: The bill would have removed tracts in the Santa Maria Basin and Santa Barbara Channel from new leasing, cutting off new drilling opportunities the Interior Department had listed for 1992-1997 [S2][S3]. Offshore drilling in these waters puts spill risk on nearby coastal communities, so the industry's interest in the tracts ran against the coast's interest in protection.

industries.industry: Coastal tourism and commercial fishing (Santa Barbara and Channel Islands region)
industries.note: Keeping the tracts off the leasing map protects the beaches, waters, and marine sanctuary that the local tourism and fishing economies depend on [S3]. The bill's benefit to these industries is the same protection it gives residents.
